newsitem.title: GREECE: Greek president to swear in new government.
newsitem.headline: Greek president to swear in new government.

text.p: Greece's socialist Prime Minister Costas Simitis kicks off his new four-year term on Wednesday when his reformist cabinet of experienced ministers and a few new faces will be sworn in.

Despite expectations that he would heavily infuse his government with young blood to tackle the country's economic problems and bring it up to speed with its European Union partners, Simitis opted for mostly experienced performers.
"(We) are called to face the country's critical problems but at the same time to face the challenges of the times and open new creative prospects for the country," he said in a statement.
"That is why we sought in forming this government to combine tested experience with the need of renewal," he added.

The cabinet, to be sworn in at 0800 GMT by state President Costis Stephanopoulos, includes just one new face as a full minister and mostly reshuffles members of the old guard who either supported or opposed Simitis's rise to power.

Socialist party officials said the strong showing of party hardliners in Sunday's election, the first won by the socialists without their late founding father Andreas Papandreou, may be his main hurdle in making radical changes.
"Simitis wants deep reforms but it won't be easy," a member of his former cabinet told Reuters.
The most dramatic change came from moving old-guard Gerassimos Arsenis from the defence ministry to the lighter-weight education ministry.
Simitis handed the defence portfolio to former interior minister Akis Tsohatzopoulos, his opponent in the tough leadership battle that followed the ailing Papandreou's resignation in January.
But Tsohatzopoulos threw his weight behind Simitis after he won the party leadership after Papandreou's death in June.

Papandreou's son George, former education minister, who was heavily favoured to replace outspoken Theodoros Pangalos at the foreign ministry, was named only deputy minister in charge of European affairs.

Simitis managed to keep his economic team largely intact, losing only Finance Minister Alexandros Papadopoulos to the interior ministry. Papadopoulos, a proven tax collector, had long expressed the wish to move from the tough ministry.
National economy minister Yannos Papandoniou will also take over finance and responsibility for next year's budget, while Development Minister Vasso Papandreou keeps her ministry.

The economic crew is credited with cutting inflation from double digits to 8.5 percent in August and attacking tax evasion but are weak on privatisations and have a poor record in attracting foreign investments.

Two private casinos, among the most important foreign investments in the past two years, fought with Papandreou who wants to impose restrictions on their operation by altering already signed contracts.
Simitis has called for "leaps ahead" to bring Greece's ailing economy around, to boost growth and to enable it to join the European Monetary Union some time after 1999.
